title: Understanding C++ and How Programs Become Executables
author: Dr. Charles Dorner

slides.title: C++ Foundations
keyPoints: Chapter 1
Understanding C++ and How Programs Become Executables
Dr. Charles Dorner
slides.narration: Welcome to Book I, C++ Foundations. In this lecture, we are going to follow a C++ program from the text we write to the process that actually runs on a computer. Our central question is simple: what happened between saving a file and seeing output? That question matters because a successful-looking result can be misleading. You can run an old executable after a new build fails. You can create an object file successfully and still have no runnable program. By the end of this lecture, you should be able to identify the stage, name the artifact it produces, and explain the evidence behind a successful run. We will use the chapter's own examples and several small, controlled failures.
actions: Open Presenter notes for the verbatim script and private directions. Keep notes closed on the audience display.
Advance with Next or the right arrow; click controls to explore examples without leaving Slides.

question.prompt: You saved main.cpp. What exists now?
question.answer: A source file exists. Saving it has not, by itself, compiled, linked, or executed the program.

slides.title: What you will be able to explain
keyPoints: The role of C++ in a software system
The artifact produced by each build stage
The selected language mode and compiler
Why a build or run failed
slides.narration: There are four outcomes for today. First, explain where C++ fits when software needs both useful abstractions and control over resources. Second, distinguish preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking by their outputs. Third, identify the compiler and the selected language mode instead of relying on a default. Fourth, use the evidence to distinguish a build failure from a running program that reports a failure. I am not expecting you to memorize every line of the sensor example today. Some syntax belongs to later chapters. Today, that example shows what C++ can express. Our detailed hands-on work will use a much smaller program so the build process stays visible.
actions: Ask learners to predict the difference between a source file, an object file, and an executable.
Reveal the answer after accepting two or three predictions.

question.prompt: Which of these is enough to prove an executable exists: saving source, producing main.o, or completing a successful link?
question.answer: A successful link to the named output establishes that the build produced an executable. Saving source and producing an object file do not.

question.prompt: What should you do before clicking Run?
question.answer: Predict the relevant output, failure stage, or exit status. Then compare the actual result with that prediction.

slides.title: Systems and application responsibilities
keyPoints: Separate the task from the mechanism
Choose a feature because a requirement needs it
slides.narration: The book introduces HarborWorks, which needs software to summarize equipment readings. An application responsibility expresses the task: which readings count, how they are summarized, and what the report means. A systems responsibility deals with facilities such as memory, files, communication, or hardware access. These responsibilities can appear in the same program. A calculation that averages accepted readings should remain understandable without knowing how a particular device was opened. C++ can support both layers, but that does not mean every component needs pointers or direct operating-system calls. The chapter asks us to name a requirement before choosing a feature. A small inventory report may benefit more from clear validation than from complicated memory management.
actions: Read both responsibilities aloud. Ask learners to classify a rule that excludes failed sensors.
Reveal the answer and connect it to the HarborWorks requirement.

comparisons.label: Application responsibility
comparisons.text: Decide which HarborWorks equipment readings belong in the report and what their summary means.

comparisons.label: Systems responsibility
comparisons.text: Arrange memory, file access, communication, or device interaction so the program can obtain and process bytes.

question.prompt: Is excluding failed sensors an application rule or a device-access mechanism?
question.answer: An application rule. Opening a device or reading its bytes is a systems mechanism. Both responsibilities can occur in the same program.

slides.title: The sensor example
keyPoints: Input order: 3, 1, 2
Ordering rule: compare each reading’s id
Output order: 1, 2, 3
Each value stays with its identifier
slides.narration: Here is the chapter's sensor example. A Reading keeps an integer identifier together with a measured value. A vector holds three readings. The sorting operation uses a comparison rule that orders them by identifier, and the loop prints each identifier with its value. Before running the program, predict the first output line. The reading with identifier one has value twenty point one, so the first line is one, colon, twenty point one. Sorting changes the order of the complete readings. It does not sort the identifiers independently and leave the values behind. You will study structures, containers, and the comparison syntax later. For now, notice how the standard library lets us express the task without writing our own allocation or sorting machinery.
actions: Before Run, ask which complete reading should print first.
Run the identifier version and compare with the prediction.
Select Order by measured value, predict again, then run. Restore Order by identifier afterward.
slides.sourceRef: B01-L0003 · Value-Type Sensor Processing with Standard Containers

variants.label: Order by identifier
Order by measured value

question.prompt: What changes when the comparator uses a.value < b.value?
question.answer: The complete readings sort by measured value: 3:18.2, then 2:19.4, then 1:20.1. Each identifier stays paired with its original value.

slides.title: The sensor example as a diagram
keyPoints: The vector owns complete Reading values
The comparator supplies ordering policy
The loop visits the reordered values
Invariant: each identifier stays with its value
slides.narration: Read this relationship map alongside the sensor example we just ran. The vector owns the readings. The comparison function supplies the ordering policy to the sorting operation. The final loop visits the reordered values. These are three different responsibilities: own the data, decide the order, and show the result. The relationship between the sort and the comparison is a dependency, not inheritance. The invariant is that each identifier remains paired with its original measured value. When we changed the comparison to use value, the order changed while the pairs remained intact. That is what a useful diagram or relationship map should help us verify. Connect each relationship back to a specific source line; do not treat the visual as a substitute for reading the program.
actions: Point to each relationship in the diagram and identify its corresponding line in the previous example. Use Open large diagram to enlarge it.
Ask learners what must stay true after either sort.

comparisons.label: Data ownership
comparisons.text: std::vector<Reading> stores the three Reading values. Reordering moves complete values, not detached identifiers.

comparisons.label: Ordering dependency
comparisons.text: std::sort asks the comparison function whether one Reading belongs before another. The relationship is a dependency, not inheritance.

comparisons.label: Observation
comparisons.text: The range-based loop prints each resulting id:value pair. The output reveals the chosen ordering rule.

question.prompt: What is the invariant across both ordering policies?
question.answer: A Reading’s identifier and measured value remain paired. Changing order must not attach a measurement to a different identifier.

slides.title: Build stages and their artifacts
keyPoints: Each stage has a different job
Each boundary has a named artifact
Running happens after the build
slides.narration: Now we move to the main concept of the chapter: the build pipeline. We begin with a source file and the headers it includes. Preprocessing handles directives and produces the translation input. Compilation translates that input into lower-level instructions. In the staged GCC demonstration, we request assembly text. Assembly produces an object file containing machine code and metadata. Linking combines the required objects and libraries to create an executable. These are conceptual boundaries even when one compiler-driver command performs several steps. Running the executable comes afterward. It is not a fifth build stage. When something fails, ask which step was attempted and which new artifact should have appeared. That question is much more useful than treating every diagnostic as the same kind of error.
actions: Select each stage from left to right. Ask for its output filename before revealing its details.
State that the displayed observations are representative; these controls do not run a local shell.
slides.sourceRef: Chapter 1, section 1.2; Preprocess, Compile, Assemble, and Link One Program

stages.label: Preprocess
stages.description: Expands preprocessing directives and included headers into translation input. The .ii file is generated C++ text.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.ii is C++ text containing header material and the program body. A successful command can produce no terminal output.

stages.label: Compile
stages.description: Checks and translates the preprocessed C++ into assembly text for the target.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.s is assembly text. Instruction names and contents depend on compiler, target, and options.

stages.label: Assemble
stages.description: Converts assembly into an object file. It may still refer to definitions that must be resolved during linking.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.o is a relocatable object. It is not yet a linked executable.

stages.label: Link
stages.description: Combines objects with required libraries to produce an executable. Only then can the operating system launch it.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/app is a linked executable. Running ./build/app is a separate operation.

question.prompt: Is running the program a fifth build stage?
question.answer: No. Preprocessing, compilation, assembly, and linking produce the executable. Running starts a process afterward.

slides.title: Preprocessing
keyPoints: Directives act before runtime
Headers contribute to the translation unit
Generated text belongs in the build folder
slides.narration: Preprocessing happens before the program runs. A directive such as include makes header contents available to translation. It does not tell the running program to open a file named iostream. In a traditional header-based build, the translation unit includes your source together with the material contributed by preprocessing. That is why a very short source file can produce a much larger preprocessed file. We will request that file with the capital E option. You only need to observe the artifact and recognize that it is text. You do not need to read the entire standard library. Keep the original source as the file you edit, and treat preprocessed output as something the tools can regenerate.
actions: Select Preprocess and point to the capital -E and the .ii output.
Explain why the generated file can be much larger than the authored source.

stages.label: Preprocess
stages.description: Expands preprocessing directives and included headers into translation input. The .ii file is generated C++ text.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.ii is C++ text containing header material and the program body. A successful command can produce no terminal output.

code.text:
mkdir -p build
g++ -std=c++20 -E main.cpp -o build/main.ii
file build/main.ii

question.prompt: Does #include <iostream> tell the running program to open a file named iostream?
question.answer: No. It is handled as part of preprocessing and translation before runtime.

slides.title: Compilation and assembly
keyPoints: Compilation checks the translation unit
Assembly text describes machine instructions
An object file can still need other definitions
slides.narration: Compilation checks the translation unit according to the selected language rules. An undeclared name or a missing semicolon usually stops progress at this stage. With the capital S option, our demonstration requests assembly text. The next command assembles that text into an object file. The lowercase c option means stop before linking. When used directly on a C++ source file, that option allows the earlier translation steps and produces an object file. The object can contain machine code, but it can still refer to definitions elsewhere. Therefore, a successful compile-only command does not promise a complete runnable program. Do not try to read the object as ordinary prose in your editor.
actions: Select Compile, then Assemble. Contrast assembly text with the object file.
Point out that -c used on a .cpp file includes earlier translation steps but still stops before linking.

stages.label: Compile
stages.description: Checks and translates the preprocessed C++ into assembly text for the target.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.s is assembly text. Instruction names and contents depend on compiler, target, and options.

stages.label: Assemble
stages.description: Converts assembly into an object file. It may still refer to definitions that must be resolved during linking.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.o is a relocatable object. It is not yet a linked executable.

code.text:
g++ -std=c++20 -S build/main.ii -o build/main.s
g++ -c build/main.s -o build/main.o

question.prompt: Can main.o exist even when no executable has been linked?
question.answer: Yes. A compile-only build intentionally stops at the object-file boundary. That object may still need definitions supplied during linking.

slides.title: Linking
keyPoints: A declaration describes a callable function
A definition supplies its implementation
The linker must receive the needed definitions
slides.narration: Linking answers a different question from compilation. Suppose a source file declares a function named total and calls it. The declaration can provide enough information for the compiler to check the call. The linker still needs the function's definition. If no supplied object or library provides it, the link can fail with an unresolved reference. That is why adding a declaration alone does not finish an implementation. In our ordinary C++ workflow, use the C++ driver for linking so it supplies the usual runtime and library choices for the environment. Later chapters examine multiple files in depth. Today, we only need the distinction: acceptable translation units can still form an incomplete program.
actions: Select Link and identify the input object and output executable.
Ask what is missing if a declared, called function has no supplied definition.

stages.label: Link
stages.description: Combines objects with required libraries to produce an executable. Only then can the operating system launch it.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/app is a linked executable. Running ./build/app is a separate operation.

question.prompt: Is a declaration enough to complete a function used by the program?
question.answer: No. A declaration can let the compiler check a call, but the program must also supply the required definition. Linking can fail when it is absent.

slides.title: Executable file and running process
keyPoints: Build success and run success are separate observations
An executable can remain after its process exits
slides.narration: An executable and a process are related, but they are different things. The executable is a file produced by the build. When the operating system starts it, a process runs with resources and execution state. After that process exits, the executable file can still remain on disk. We can launch it again without rebuilding, which is useful and also explains the stale-executable problem we will demonstrate. Output tells us something about a particular run. The exit status tells the shell whether the program reported success or failure according to its convention. A successful build and a successful run are separate observations. Neither one, by itself, proves that the current source satisfies every requirement.
actions: Ask whether launching the executable again requires another build.
Reveal the answer, then connect it to the stale-executable demonstration later in the lecture.

comparisons.label: Executable file
comparisons.text: The build output on disk, such as build/app. It can remain after a run finishes.

comparisons.label: Running process
comparisons.text: A launched instance with execution state and resources managed by the operating system.

question.prompt: If app has already run and exited, can you launch it again without rebuilding?
question.answer: Yes, if the executable file remains usable. That convenience is also why an older executable may still run after a later build fails.

slides.title: Language standard and implementation
keyPoints: C++20 is this book’s host baseline
-std=c++20 selects the GCC/Clang language mode
__cplusplus reports the selected mode
One successful program is a narrow check
slides.narration: The C++ standard describes language and library behavior. A compiler toolchain implements that contract. This book deliberately uses C++20 as its baseline for host examples. That choice does not mean every example requires a feature introduced in C++20, and it is not a claim about the newest standard. Specify the mode explicitly instead of relying on a compiler's default. The predefined macro named underscore underscore cplusplus reports a language-mode value. Our program compares it with twenty twenty zero two, written numerically as 202002. A conforming C++20 report uses that value. This check tells us about the selected mode. It does not establish support for every library facility, and it is not a performance measurement.
actions: Read the distinction between a language standard and an implementation.
Emphasize that the book chooses C++20 as a baseline, not as a statement about the newest standard.

question.prompt: Does __cplusplus >= 202002L establish that every required library feature works?
question.answer: No. It reports the selected language mode and satisfies this program’s numeric threshold. Specific compiler and library facilities still need appropriate checks.

slides.title: Compiler families and build reports
keyPoints: Compiler options differ across implementations
Report the compiler, target, and exact command
slides.narration: GCC, Clang, and Microsoft Visual C++ are different compiler implementations. Their options, diagnostics, and platform integration can differ. GCC and Clang commonly accept the dash std equals c plus plus twenty option. MSVC uses its own slash option, and the cplusplus macro may also require slash Zc colon underscore underscore cplusplus to report the selected mode as expected. We will use GCC with a Bash-like shell in this lecture. Do not translate those commands to Windows simply by changing the compiler name. A useful build report records the compiler and version, the library implementation when relevant, the target platform, and the exact command. Preserve the earliest useful diagnostic and enough source to reproduce the problem.
actions: Compare the language-mode options without implying all shell commands are interchangeable.
Ask which missing detail makes a build report hard to reproduce.

comparisons.label: GCC / Clang
comparisons.text: Select the book’s mode with -std=c++20. Record compiler version and relevant standard-library implementation.

comparisons.label: Microsoft Visual C++
comparisons.text: Use /std:c++20. Correct __cplusplus reporting may also require /Zc:__cplusplus.

comparisons.label: A reproducible report
comparisons.text: Include source, compiler version, platform, full command, output path, and the earliest useful diagnostic.

question.prompt: Why is “it fails in C++” an incomplete build report?
question.answer: It omits the implementation, version, language mode, target, source, command, and diagnostic. Those details determine what another person can reproduce.

slides.title: The chapter’s language-mode probe
keyPoints: #ifndef is handled before runtime
The ordinary if statement runs inside main
The two output streams serve different purposes
slides.narration: This is the complete worked program from Chapter 1. The include provides the declarations needed for stream output. The preprocessing check asks whether the cplusplus macro exists. Inside main, the program prints an explanatory sentence and the macro's value. The ordinary if statement executes when the program runs. If the mode value is below the chapter's baseline, it writes a message to standard error and returns one. Otherwise, it prints PASS. Reaching the end of main returns success. Notice that the preprocessing conditional and the runtime if occur at different stages. This program deliberately permits a C++17 build so that its runtime check can reject that mode. We will observe both cases rather than guessing what the build command did.
actions: Point to #ifndef, the __cplusplus print, the runtime if, and the final PASS.
Ask learners to distinguish the preprocessing conditional from the ordinary if.
Run once in C++20 mode if helpful, leaving the source unchanged.

code.expectedStdout:
A source file becomes an executable.
__cplusplus=202002
PASS

question.prompt: Why can this example compile in C++17 but still report a failure when run?
question.answer: Its syntax is valid in C++17. Its ordinary runtime if then detects that __cplusplus is below the chosen C++20 threshold, writes to standard error, and returns 1.

slides.title: A complete build and run
keyPoints: Expected GCC C++20 output
A source file becomes an executable.
__cplusplus=202002
PASS
slides.narration: We now run the complete example with the book’s C++20 language mode. Before clicking Run, predict the sentence, the language-mode value, and PASS. The expected C++20 macro value is 202002, and the successful path returns zero. The result panel reports the actual compilation and execution response from the online runner when that service is available. The expected-output panel is a reference, not proof of a new run. Keep those two kinds of evidence separate. On a local Bash terminal, the equivalent guarded sequence is g plus plus with the selected options, followed by double ampersand and the executable path. The double ampersand allows execution only after a successful build. PASS proves this program’s explicit check passed; it does not certify every compiler feature or the correctness of every application.
actions: Predict the sentence, mode value, PASS, and zero exit status.
Click Run and compare actual output with the expected baseline.
Explain that this Run submits source to the existing online runner; local shell commands have different controls.

code.expectedStdout:
A source file becomes an executable.
__cplusplus=202002
PASS

question.prompt: What does PASS prove here?
question.answer: This execution reached the success path after checking __cplusplus against 202002L. It does not prove complete library support or overall application correctness.

slides.title: Demonstration: intermediate files
keyPoints: main.cpp     Authored source
main.ii         Preprocessed text
main.s          Assembly text
main.o          Object file
app                Linked executable
slides.narration: Use this interactive build walkthrough to stop at each boundary. First, preprocessing creates main dot ii. Next, compilation creates assembly text in main dot s. Assembly creates main dot o. Finally, linking creates app. Before selecting each stage, name the artifact you expect. The panel describes a representative observation; it has not executed these shell commands or generated those files in your browser. To collect real local evidence, copy the sequence into a Bash terminal in a folder containing the chapter’s main dot cpp, with a working C++ compiler. The commands are chained so a failure stops the later steps. Do not expect an executable immediately after compile-only processing. Only after linking do we launch app. Named commands and named artifacts connect the conceptual pipeline to an observation you can verify.
actions: Select all four stages and ask learners to name each artifact before exposing the description.
Point to the copyable Bash sequence as the local verification path.
Distinguish representative walkthrough observations from an actual online Run result.

stages.label: Preprocess
stages.description: Expands preprocessing directives and included headers into translation input. The .ii file is generated C++ text.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.ii is C++ text containing header material and the program body. A successful command can produce no terminal output.

stages.label: Compile
stages.description: Checks and translates the preprocessed C++ into assembly text for the target.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.s is assembly text. Instruction names and contents depend on compiler, target, and options.

stages.label: Assemble
stages.description: Converts assembly into an object file. It may still refer to definitions that must be resolved during linking.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/main.o is a relocatable object. It is not yet a linked executable.

stages.label: Link
stages.description: Combines objects with required libraries to produce an executable. Only then can the operating system launch it.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: build/app is a linked executable. Running ./build/app is a separate operation.

code.text:
mkdir -p build
g++ -std=c++20 -E main.cpp -o build/main.ii &&
g++ -std=c++20 -S build/main.ii -o build/main.s &&
g++ -c build/main.s -o build/main.o &&
g++ build/main.o -o build/app &&
./build/app

question.prompt: Which command is the first one in this sequence that creates build/app?
question.answer: The link command, g++ build/main.o -o build/app. The earlier commands create .ii, .s, and .o artifacts.

slides.title: C++17 and C++20: different run results
keyPoints: Same source, two selected language modes
C++20: expected PASS and exit 0
C++17: expected rejection and exit 1
slides.narration: Now we change just the selected language mode. The source remains the same. The C++20 build prints PASS and returns success. The C++17 build can also compile and link because this small program does not require C++20-only syntax. When that executable runs, its explicit check finds the older mode, prints the rejection message, and returns one. That is an intentional runtime rejection, not a compiler error. The distinction matters: a nonzero exit status can be a designed response to a condition. Also remember that standard output and standard error are separate streams. A tool that captures them separately may display their text in a different arrangement. Compare the message content and the exit status.
actions: Select C++20 mode and Run.
Select C++17 mode without editing the source; predict the rejection, then Run.
Compare standard output, standard error, and the program exit status. Restore C++20 afterward.
slides.sourceRef: B01-L0010; Chapter 1, Read the result at the correct level

code.expectedStdout:
A source file becomes an executable.
__cplusplus=202002
PASS

variants.label: C++20 mode
C++17 mode

comparisons.label: C++20 expectation
comparisons.text: stdout includes __cplusplus=202002 and PASS; stderr is empty; program exit status is 0.

comparisons.label: C++17 expectation
comparisons.text: stdout includes __cplusplus=201703 without PASS; stderr says Select C++20 or later for this series.; program exit status is 1.

question.prompt: The C++17 program returns 1. Did compilation necessarily fail?
question.answer: No. This program can compile and link in C++17, then intentionally reject the selected mode at runtime.

slides.title: Failure during compilation
keyPoints: Controlled defect: a missing semicolon
Read the first useful diagnostic
No successful new build to run
Repair the source, then rebuild
slides.narration: Our first controlled failure removes a semicolon from an output statement in a copy of the program. The compiler should reject the source. Read the first useful diagnostic and its source location. Do not expect every compiler version to use identical wording, and do not assume the first displayed line is always the root cause. The key observation is that the new translation failed. We must repair the source and build again before claiming the changed program ran. Notice that we use a separate demonstration file so the correct example stays intact. In a real project, preserve a small reproducer and the exact failing command. That evidence makes a report much easier for someone else to investigate.
actions: Run the Missing semicolon variant and read the first useful compiler diagnostic.
Explain that a compiler failure is not the same as a program returning 1.
Select Restore semicolon and run again to verify the repaired source.
slides.sourceRef: Chapter 1, A misleading success: the stale executable; controlled teaching variation of B01-L0010

code.expectedStderr: Representative diagnostic: expected ; before } token. Actual compiler wording and source locations vary.

variants.label: Missing semicolon
Restore semicolon

question.prompt: Why is it wrong to describe the failed build as “the program ran and returned 1”?
question.answer: The source was rejected during compilation, so this request did not reach program execution. A service may separately report a compiler status; that is not a program exit status.

slides.title: Failure during linking
keyPoints: Compile-only command succeeds
The call has a declaration
The definition is absent from the link
Adding the defining object completes the program
slides.narration: This file declares total and calls it, but does not define it. A compile-only command can succeed because the declaration tells the compiler how the call is formed. Linking that object by itself fails because the required definition is missing. Select the walkthrough stages to compare those boundaries. The online Run action requests a complete program build, so its declaration-only variant should fail at linking. Select Definition included to see the smallest one-file repair. In a multi-file project, the equivalent repair can be to compile total dot cpp and supply its object to the link. Do not memorize a particular unresolved-reference message. Learn the distinction between a name that was never declared and a declared function whose required definition is absent from the linked program.
actions: Select Compile the call, then Link without definition, then Supply the definition. Identify these as representative local stages.
Run Declaration only to request an actual complete online build.
Run Definition included and explain that the successful program returns 0 with no printed output.

stages.label: Compile the call
stages.description: caller.cpp contains int total(); followed by int main() { return total(); }. The declaration makes the call checkable.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: compile-only translation succeeds and creates caller.o.

stages.label: Link without definition
stages.description: No linked object or library supplies a definition of total().
stages.recordedOutput: Representative diagnostic, not execution: undefined reference to total(). Exact wording differs by linker.

stages.label: Supply the definition
stages.command: g++ -std=c++20 -c total.cpp -o build/total.o && g++ build/caller.o build/total.o -o build/caller
stages.description: total.cpp contains int total() { return 0; }. The link now receives both object files.
stages.recordedOutput: Representative observation, not execution: linking succeeds. Running ./build/caller then returns 0 and prints nothing.

code.text:
int total();
int main() { return total(); }
code.expectedStderr: Representative linker diagnostic: undefined reference to total().

variants.label: Declaration only
variants.text:
int total();
int main() { return total(); }

variants.label: Definition included

question.prompt: If total.cpp exists in your editor, does that alone prove the linker received its definition?
question.answer: No. Check that it was compiled and that the resulting object, or another object or library with the definition, participated in the link.

slides.title: Build success and behavior correctness
keyPoints: Compilation failure: invalid source
Link failure: missing required definition
Runtime rejection: the program returns failure
Logic error: the result violates the requirement
slides.narration: We now have enough evidence to separate several categories. A missing semicolon can stop compilation. A missing function definition can stop linking. Our C++17 probe can build successfully and then intentionally report a failure while running. A logic error is another possibility: the program builds and runs but produces a result that violates its requirement. For example, sorting readings by identifier would be wrong if the actual requirement were to sort by measured value. A clean build does not decide whether we selected the right business rule. When diagnosing a problem, state the requirement, identify the stage, and compare the observed artifact or behavior with the expected one.
actions: Read each scenario before revealing its classification.
Ask learners to justify the stage by naming the evidence.

checks.question: A semicolon is missing and the source is rejected. Which boundary?
checks.answer: Compilation: the source does not meet the selected language rules.

checks.question: A called function has a declaration but no supplied definition. Which boundary?
checks.answer: Linking: the complete program is missing a required definition.

checks.question: The C++17 probe builds, prints its rejection, and returns 1. Which boundary?
checks.answer: Runtime: the program intentionally rejects the selected language mode.

checks.question: Readings sort by identifier, but the requirement says sort by value. Which problem?
checks.answer: A logic or requirement error: successful building and running do not prove the selected rule was correct.

slides.title: The stale executable trap
keyPoints: This is a step-by-step model, not a browser shell
A failed compile may leave an older executable
A guarded command skips the run after build failure
slides.narration: Walk through this model one step at a time. We first build a valid executable. Then we remove a semicolon from the current source and try to rebuild. Compilation fails before a replacement executable is linked, so the earlier file can remain. If we launch that existing file separately, it can still print PASS. The edited source did not become valid; we ran a file left from an earlier successful build. Finally, consider the same failing build followed by double ampersand and the run command. Bash skips the run because the build failed. These steps are labeled as a model, not the output of a browser shell. To demonstrate the trap locally, use a throwaway copy of the example. The reasoning stays the same: connect the source path, the successful build, and the executable actually launched.
actions: Advance through one sequence step at a time. Pause before the separate run and ask learners to predict its output.
Before the guarded command, ask whether Bash will launch the old file.
Emphasize that this is a model; it does not inspect or modify any local executable.
slides.sourceRef: Chapter 1, A misleading success: the stale executable

sequence.label: Build version A
sequence.observation: Model: the valid source builds. build/app is version A and can print PASS.

sequence.label: Break the current source
sequence.command: # Remove the semicolon after the PASS statement.
sequence.observation: Model: the edited source is now invalid. Editing source alone does not replace build/app.

sequence.label: Try rebuilding
sequence.observation: Model: compilation fails before a replacement executable is linked. The previous build/app can remain.

sequence.label: Run the old file separately
sequence.observation: Model: the existing version A executable runs and prints its old PASS. The edited source has not built successfully.

sequence.label: Guard execution with build success
sequence.observation: Model: the build fails, so Bash skips the right-hand command. This guarded sequence does not launch the old program.

question.prompt: Does old PASS establish that the edited source compiled?
question.answer: No. It may come from a previously built executable. Require a successful current build and verify the executable path.

slides.title: Evidence for a reproducible claim
keyPoints: Source file and deliberate change
Compiler version and complete command
Named output artifact
Observed output and immediate exit status
slides.narration: A useful claim about software includes enough evidence to reproduce it. We can say that we changed a particular message in a particular source file, built it with the displayed command, and ran the executable at the displayed path. Then we compare the new output with our prediction. Recording the compiler version and environment narrows the conditions of the claim. A screenshot showing PASS alone omits most of that information. For today's lab, keep a short evidence log. State the requested stopping point, the resulting filename, and whether linking or execution has happened. The goal is a clear connection between the authored source and the behavior we observe, with no hidden jump to an unrelated executable.
actions: Ask learners to write a one-sentence claim connecting a named source, command, output artifact, and observation.
Reveal the example and identify the limits of the claim.
slides.sourceRef: Chapter 1, Guided lab — Build an evidence trail

question.prompt: Rewrite “It worked” as a reproducible claim.
question.answer: Example: With the recorded GCC version, I built the named main.cpp using g++ -std=c++20 main.cpp -o build/app, then ran ./build/app; it printed my changed sentence and returned 0. Include the actual output and environment in the log.

slides.title: Guided lab: a build evidence trail
keyPoints: Predict before each build step
Create .ii, .s, .o, and the executable locally
Change one sentence and verify new output
Explain a missing link and a guarded failed build
slides.narration: Now repeat the pipeline and collect your own evidence. The command panel provides a local Bash sequence for a folder containing the chapter’s main dot cpp and an installed C++ compiler. It creates generated files under build slash pipeline-lab. Before executing each stage, write the filename you expect and whether linking or execution has happened. Next, change only the printed sentence, rebuild, and confirm that the executable shows your change. Explain what is missing if you stop after the object file. Finally, try a throwaway missing-semicolon copy with a guarded build-and-run command and explain why the run is skipped. The online editor can verify the changed sentence, but it does not supply the local intermediate-file evidence. Pause here while learners perform the sequence, then use the checks to compare their reasoning.
actions: Copy the command sequence only when learners are ready to use their own local terminal.
Allow a pause for the evidence log. Keep this slide available as the instructions.
Reveal the checks after learners have recorded predictions and observations.
slides.sourceRef: Chapter 1, Guided lab — Build an evidence trail

code.text:
mkdir -p build/pipeline-lab
g++ -std=c++20 -E main.cpp -o build/pipeline-lab/main.ii &&
g++ -std=c++20 -S build/pipeline-lab/main.ii -o build/pipeline-lab/main.s &&
g++ -c build/pipeline-lab/main.s -o build/pipeline-lab/main.o &&
g++ build/pipeline-lab/main.o -o build/pipeline-lab/app &&
./build/pipeline-lab/app

checks.question: What proves the deliberate source change reached the executed program?
checks.answer: A successful rebuild from the changed source followed by running its named output executable and observing the changed sentence.

checks.question: If only main.o exists, what is still required?
checks.answer: A successful link with required objects and libraries to create the executable; then a separate run.

checks.question: What should a guarded failed build do?
checks.answer: Skip the run command on the right of && because the build command returned failure.

slides.title: Review in Study Studio
keyPoints: State the answer before revealing it
Explain the artifact or behavior that supports it
Use Chapter scope in Flashcards for later review
slides.narration: Use these review prompts before looking at their answers. The goal is retrieval followed by an explanation, not simply recognizing a phrase. Name the stage and the evidence. After this lecture, open Flashcards in Study Studio and choose Chapter scope for more practice. Saved study state can affect the card order, so focus on the concept rather than a particular card number. In Practice, record your prediction or evidence before comparing it with the source explanation. Review marks are self-assessments that help organize study. They do not replace a successful build, an observed artifact, or a clear explanation of a failed step. If a distinction remains uncertain, revisit the corresponding slide and vary one thing at a time.
actions: Read each prompt and wait for an explanation before revealing its answer.
After the lecture, direct learners to Flashcards with Chapter scope and then Practice.

checks.question: Which generated artifact is expanded C++ text?
checks.answer: The preprocessed .ii file in this GCC demonstration.

checks.question: Which artifact may contain machine code but still need definitions elsewhere?
checks.answer: The object file, such as main.o.

checks.question: Can an executable remain after its process finishes?
checks.answer: Yes. The running process ends; the executable file can stay on disk.

slides.title: Exit questions
keyPoints: Can main.o exist without an executable?
What does a missing definition usually affect?
Does old PASS prove the edited source built?
What does the language-mode probe actually prove?
slides.narration: Before we finish, answer these four questions. Can the object file exist without an executable? Yes. A compile-only command deliberately stops before linking. What does a missing function definition usually affect when a compatible declaration was available? Linking, because the required definition must be supplied. Does an old PASS prove the edited source built successfully? No. The executable may be left from an earlier build. Finally, what does the language-mode probe actually prove? It reports the selected mode and checks whether that numeric value reaches the program's threshold. It does not establish complete library support or overall application correctness. If you can explain those answers using our demonstrations, you have the central model this chapter is trying to teach.
actions: Ask learners to answer all four questions without consulting earlier slides.
Reveal each answer and request the supporting demonstration.

checks.question: Can main.o exist without an executable?
checks.answer: Yes. A compile-only command stops before linking.

checks.question: What does a missing required definition usually affect when a compatible declaration exists?
checks.answer: Linking. The definition must be supplied by a linked object or library.

checks.question: Does old PASS prove the edited source built?
checks.answer: No. An earlier executable may still run after a later build fails.

checks.question: What does this language-mode probe actually establish?
checks.answer: It reports __cplusplus and checks its numeric value against the program’s C++20 threshold. It does not prove every library feature or overall correctness.

slides.title: Chapter 1 assignment
keyPoints: Submit commands, artifacts, and observations
Classify one compile failure and one link failure
Explain one stale-executable result
Next: a complete C++ development environment
slides.narration: For your assignment, submit the build evidence log and a short explanation of the controlled failures. Include the commands that create the intermediate artifacts, the successful command that builds your changed program, and the resulting output and exit status. Explain which stage failed in the semicolon example and which stage failed in the missing-definition example. Then explain why an old executable could still run and how the guarded shell command changes that behavior. You do not need identical diagnostic wording or identical file sizes to demonstrate understanding. You need accurate stage names and a reproducible connection between source and execution. Chapter 2 develops the complete development environment. Our takeaway today is to name the stage, inspect its artifact, and verify which executable actually ran.
actions: Review the submission requirements and invite learners to export or copy their evidence log.
Use Previous to revisit an uncertain boundary before ending the lecture.

checks.question: What belongs in the evidence log?
checks.answer: Source identification and deliberate change; compiler version and platform; full commands; named artifacts; actual output, diagnostics, and immediate exit status where relevant.

checks.question: How should the two controlled failures be explained?
checks.answer: Missing semicolon: compilation fails. Declared but undefined function: complete linking fails. Use actual observations and allow compiler-specific diagnostic wording.

checks.question: What is the explanation for an old successful result?
checks.answer: A previous executable remained and was launched separately. A build followed by && and the run command skips execution when that build fails.

question.prompt: What is the habit to carry into Chapter 2?
question.answer: Name the stage, inspect its artifact, and verify which executable actually ran.
